transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess I’m here because I just feel wound up almost all the time. Like my body is constantly bracing for something bad to happen, even when nothing is actually happening. I can be sitting at my desk doing normal computer support stuff, and I’ll notice my shoulders are tight and I feel like I’m waiting for the next problem to drop.

And it’s not just at work, which is part of why I thought I should come in. Even when I’m trying to relax or do something fun, like going to dance night, I still feel tense, like I can’t fully settle into it. It’s kind of exhausting, honestly, because there isn’t always a clear reason for it. It’s just this constant “on edge” feeling in my body.
Have you ever had a sudden episode where you felt an intense fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes?

I don’t think so, not in that way. I mean, I definitely get really uncomfortable and tense, and sometimes it feels like my body is on high alert, but I wouldn’t say it suddenly spikes into this really intense fear that peaks within a few minutes.

It’s more like… it builds or just stays there in the background, if that makes sense. Like a constant hum rather than a sudden wave crashing over me. I don’t usually have a specific moment where I’m like, “Oh no, this is happening right now,” and then it reaches a peak fast. At least, not that I’ve noticed.
Do you find yourself having recurring thoughts or ideas that you can't seem to get out of your head?

Yes, definitely. It’s not usually like one strange thought popping in out of nowhere, it’s more like the same worries get stuck on a loop. Like at work, I’ll send an email or update a spreadsheet, and even after I’ve checked it—sometimes more than once—I’ll still be thinking, “What if I missed something? What if I sent it to the wrong person? What if there’s an error and someone catches it later?”

And then it doesn’t just stay as that one thought. It kind of branches out. One “what if” turns into five more before I can pull myself back. I’ll tell myself, “You already checked this, it’s fine,” but it doesn’t really land right away. The thought keeps circling, and I have to keep mentally arguing with it, which gets really tiring.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or activities because of these worries or feelings of tension?

Yeah… I have, and I think that’s part of what finally made me feel like this isn’t just “normal stress” or me being dramatic.

At work, I’ve started falling behind on support tickets because I get stuck double-checking really simple things. Like, I’ll be resolving something routine or updating notes, and then I’ll keep going back over it to make sure I didn’t miss a detail or word something wrong. And while I’m doing that, new tickets are still coming in, obviously, so then I get more behind, and that makes me even more tense. A couple of coworkers have had to pick up the slack, which feels awful because I don’t want to be that person who isn’t carrying her part.

And outside of work, yes, I’ve been avoiding things too. I’ve skipped several dance nights, even though I usually like going, because by the time it comes around I just feel too overwhelmed to show up and be around people. Same with mentoring sessions—I’ve missed some of those too. I’ll tell myself I’m just tired or that I’ll go next time, but really it’s that I feel like I can’t handle another thing, even if it’s something I normally care about.
Do you have any repetitive behaviors that you feel compelled to do?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I don’t think I have, like, rituals exactly, if that’s what you mean. I don’t feel like I have to tap things a certain number of times or arrange things in a specific way or anything like that.

I do re-check things, but it feels more tied to worrying that I made a mistake than to a specific behavior I’m compelled to do in a particular pattern. Like I’ll go back and look at something again because I’m afraid I missed something, not because I feel like something bad will happen if I don’t do it in the “right” way, if that makes sense.

So… maybe some checking, but I don’t know if I’d call it repetitive behavior in the way you mean. It’s more like I can’t feel settled until I’ve reassured myself, and even then it doesn’t always stick.
Do you often worry about everyday things, such as finances, relationships, or health, even when there's no apparent reason to worry?

Yes… honestly, that’s probably the biggest thing. It feels like my worry doesn’t stay in one place anymore. It used to be easier to point to one specific thing, like the condo or some practical issue, and say, “Okay, I’m stressed because of that.” But now it just jumps around all day.

Like I’ll start off wondering if my cousin is upset with me because a text sounded a little short, and then before I’ve even really sorted that out in my head, I’m thinking about whether I’m going to make a mistake on a support call at work. Then that turns into thinking about money, like how I’m ever supposed to save enough or move forward with my life in a normal way. And it’s not always because something actually happened. Sometimes nothing has changed, but my mind still finds something to latch onto.

It’s frustrating because I can sort of hear how excessive it sounds when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels very real, like each worry needs my attention right then.
Do you often feel restless or have an inability to relax, even when you're not actively worrying about something?

Yes. That’s actually one of the main reasons I came in, because I feel wound up almost all the time. It’s not just when I’m actively thinking through a specific problem, either. It’s like my body is already bracing for the next bad thing before I even know what I’m worried about.

I can be just sitting at my desk, not doing anything especially stressful, and I’ll notice I’m tense, like I’m waiting for something to go wrong or for someone to need something from me. And then even if I try to take a break or do something I normally enjoy, like going to dance night, I don’t really feel settled. I’m there, but part of me still feels keyed up, like I can’t fully relax into it.

It’s hard to explain because mentally I might not have one clear worry in that exact moment, but physically I still feel on alert. Like I’m never completely off-duty, I guess.
Have your worries or feelings of tension significantly interfered with your relationships or daily activities?

Yeah… yes, it has. I wish I could say it was mostly internal and I’m just uncomfortable, but it’s started affecting things in a more obvious way.

At work, I’ve been falling behind on support tickets, which is really embarrassing because I’m usually pretty reliable. It’s not that I don’t know how to do the tasks, exactly. It’s more like I’ll spend way too long double-checking simple things—like rereading a response before I send it, or checking whether I documented something correctly, or going back over steps I already completed because I suddenly feel unsure. And then the queue keeps moving while I’m stuck on one thing that should’ve taken a few minutes. A couple of times coworkers have had to help pick up the slack, and I feel awful about that because then I start worrying they think I’m not pulling my weight.

And outside of work, I’ve been skipping things I normally care about. Dance nights used to be something I looked forward to, like a break from everything, but lately I’ll get to the point of needing to leave and just feel too overwhelmed to go. Same with mentoring sessions—I’ve missed several because the idea of showing up and being “on” felt like too much, even though I know those are meaningful and I don’t want to be unreliable there either.

So yes, it’s definitely interfering. Not every single day in some dramatic way, but enough that I’m noticing consequences, and other people probably are too.
Have you been experiencing these worries about everyday things for more than 6 months?

Yes. It’s been more than six months. I’d say about nine months now, if I’m counting from when the condo loan started moving toward foreclosure.

That was sort of the point where the worrying stopped feeling like a normal reaction to a stressful situation and started becoming… I don’t know, like a constant background noise. At first I told myself, “Of course I’m worried, anyone would be,” because the foreclosure stuff was genuinely scary and practical and real. But then months kept going by, and even when I wasn’t dealing with that exact issue in the moment, the worry was still there and started attaching itself to everything else.

So yes, roughly nine months. It feels like long enough that I can’t really tell myself it’s just a bad week anymore.
Do you find it difficult to stop worrying about everyday things once you've started?

Yes, definitely. That’s one of the most frustrating parts, honestly, because I can tell myself logically, “You already checked that,” or “You already sent the email,” or “There’s nothing else you can do about it right now,” but it doesn’t really stop.

Like with work stuff, I’ll check a spreadsheet and see that the information is there, and then a few minutes later I’ll have this thought like, “What if I missed a row?” or “What if I typed something wrong?” And then I go back and check it again, and sometimes even after that, my brain still doesn’t feel satisfied. It’s like the worry doesn’t accept evidence, if that makes sense.

And one “what if” turns into another really quickly. I’ll start with, “What if I made a mistake in that email?” and then it becomes, “What if the person misunderstands it?” and then, “What if my manager notices?” and then, “What if everyone thinks I’m careless?” It can spiral before I even realize how far it’s gone.

I do try to pull myself back, but it takes effort, and sometimes I feel like I’m arguing with my own mind. Like I know I’m overthinking, but knowing that doesn’t automatically make it stop.
Are your worries usually about one specific type of thing, like work or finances, or do they seem to jump around between lots of different things?

It definitely jumps around. It started with the condo, because that was the big obvious thing, and for a while I could kind of point to that and say, “Okay, this is what I’m worried about.” But now it doesn’t stay there at all.

It’ll move from something financial, like how I’m ever supposed to save money or get back on track or move forward with my life, to something totally different, like whether my cousin is upset with me because she texted a little shorter than usual. And then I’ll start replaying what I said to her, wondering if I sounded dismissive or if I forgot something important.

And then at work it’ll become, “What if I make a mistake on this support call?” or “What if I don’t explain the fix clearly enough?” or “What if they think I’m incompetent?” It’s like my brain is always looking for the next place to land. So no, it’s not just one category anymore. It’s finances, relationships, work, the future—just kind of everything rotating through.
Are your worries usually about one specific area of your life, such as work or relationships?

No, it’s not usually just one area anymore. I mean, it started with the condo, so for a while I could tell myself, “This is financial stress, that makes sense.” But now it doesn’t stay there. It jumps around a lot.

Like I’ll be thinking about the condo or money, and then suddenly it turns into, “How am I ever going to save anything?” or “How am I supposed to move forward with my life if I’m always trying to catch up?” And then later the same day I’ll be stuck wondering if my cousin is upset with me because her text sounded a little short, and I’ll replay what I said to see if I did something wrong.

And at work it’ll be something else completely, like worrying I’m going to make a mistake on a support call or explain something badly and the person will think I don’t know what I’m doing. So… yeah, it moves between finances, family or relationships, work, the future. It doesn’t really stay in one lane.
Do you often notice muscle tension, such as clenching your jaw or tightening your fists, when you're feeling anxious or worried?

Yeah… I do notice that, though I don’t always catch it right away. It’s more like I’ll suddenly realize my whole body has been tense for who knows how long. Like I’m sitting at my desk, not doing anything physically stressful, just answering tickets or reading something, and my shoulders are up or my body feels kind of locked in place.

It feels like I’m wound up almost all the time, honestly. Like my body is bracing for the next bad thing even when nothing is actually happening in that moment. I could be trying to focus on work, or even doing something that’s supposed to be fun, like dance night, and there’s still this tight, on-edge feeling underneath it.

It’s not always dramatic, but it’s constant enough that I notice it. Like I’m not fully relaxed very often. My body acts like it’s waiting for something to go wrong.
Is there one particular thing that you worry about more than anything else?

I guess if I had to pick, the condo is still the one that feels like the original “big” worry, because that’s where all of this seemed to start. But it doesn’t really stay there anymore, so it’s hard to say there’s just one thing.

It’s more like the condo or money will be the doorway into everything else. I’ll start thinking about finances, like how I’m supposed to save money again or move forward with my life, and then somehow my brain jumps to something completely different. Like I’ll suddenly be worrying that my cousin is upset with me because her text sounded off, and then I’m replaying what I said and wondering if I did something wrong.

And then at work it shifts again, like, “What if I make a mistake on this support call?” or “What if I explain something badly and they think I’m incompetent?” So… the condo might be the biggest concrete thing, but honestly the worry doesn’t stay attached to one particular thing anymore. It kind of spreads out to whatever my brain can grab onto next.
Do you have any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to ignore them or make them stop?

Yeah, definitely. It’s like the thought doesn’t just come up once and then pass. It keeps circling back even after I’ve tried to reassure myself.

Like with work, I’ll tell myself, “You already sent the email, it was fine,” or “You already checked that spreadsheet,” but then a few minutes later I’m thinking, “What if I missed something?” And then that turns into, “What if someone notices before I do?” and then, “What if they think I’m careless?” and then it kind of branches out from there.

It’s frustrating because I can usually see, logically, that I’m repeating myself. I’ll know I’ve already checked something or already thought through it, but it doesn’t feel settled. My mind keeps looping back to it anyway, and one little “what if” turns into five more before I can really pull myself out of it. Sometimes I can stop it for a bit, but it’s like my brain just picks it back up again.
Are your worries usually focused on one main area of concern or do they cover a wide range of topics?

It covers a pretty wide range now. I mean, the condo was the main thing at first, and it still kind of sits in the background as this big unresolved thing, but the worry doesn’t stay neatly in that one box anymore.

It’ll start with something practical, like money or whether I’m ever going to be able to save properly again or move forward with my life, and then suddenly it’s about something totally different. Like I’ll be thinking about finances, and then my mind jumps to my cousin, like, “Was she annoyed with me?” or “Did I say something weird?” just because a text sounded a little short.

And then at work it’ll switch again. I’ll be on a support call or about to respond to someone and start thinking, “What if I make a mistake?” or “What if I explain it badly and they think I don’t know what I’m doing?” So it’s not really one main area anymore. It kind of bounces around to whatever feels like it could go wrong next.
Do you think your worries are usually about things that could realistically happen, or are they often about unlikely scenarios?

I think that’s what makes it confusing, because a lot of them are technically realistic. Like, it’s not impossible that my cousin could be upset with me, or that I could make a mistake on a support call, or that money could be tight and I’ll struggle to save again. Those things could happen.

But the way my mind treats them feels bigger than the actual situation, if that makes sense. A short text from my cousin turns into me wondering if I damaged the relationship somehow. One work call turns into, “What if I mess this up and everyone thinks I’m bad at my job?” And then the condo or money stuff becomes this whole spiral about how I’m ever going to move forward with my life.

So I wouldn’t say they’re always totally unrealistic scenarios. It’s more that my worry grabs onto things that are possible, and then it stretches them out until they feel much more threatening than they probably are.
Do you feel like you're able to control your worries most of the time?

Not most of the time, no. I can sometimes interrupt them for a little bit, but it doesn’t feel like I’m really in control of them.

Like, I’ll tell myself, “Okay, I already checked the spreadsheet,” or “I already sent that email, and it looked fine,” and I’ll try to move on. And for maybe a few minutes I can focus on something else. But then the thought comes back, almost like it was waiting there. It’s not even always a new concern — it’s the same thing looping again, like, “But what if you missed something?” or “What if you sent it with the wrong attachment?” or “What if someone notices and thinks you’re careless?”

And then once that starts, it doesn’t stay as one thought. One “what if” turns into five more before I can really pull myself back. I’ll know I’m doing it, too, which is the frustrating part. I’ll be sitting there thinking, “You already went over this,” but it still doesn’t feel settled. It’s like reassurance only works briefly, and then my mind starts arguing with it again. So I wouldn’t say I can control it most of the time. I can try to manage it, but it often feels like it keeps going on its own.
Do you usually worry about things that might happen in the future?

Yes, mostly. It’s very often about what might happen next, or what something could turn into. Like, it doesn’t just stay on the condo anymore, even though that’s still there in the background. My mind will jump ahead to, “What if I can’t save money again?” or “What if I never really get back on track or move forward with my life?”

And then it’ll jump to people, like with my cousin — if she seems a little off or sends a short reply, I start worrying that maybe she’s upset with me, and then I’m imagining what that means later, like maybe things will become awkward or I’ll have damaged the relationship somehow.

Or at work, before or during a support call, I’ll start thinking ahead like, “What if I make a mistake?” or “What if I don’t explain something clearly?” It’s not always something that has happened. It’s more like my brain keeps scanning for the next thing that could go wrong, and then I’m already reacting to it as if it’s about to happen.
Is there a particular area of your life where your worries seem to originate or concentrate most frequently?

It used to feel like the condo was the main thing, or at least that was the easiest thing to point to. Like, if someone asked me what I was stressed about, I could say, “Oh, it’s the condo situation,” and that would sound concrete.

But honestly, it doesn’t really stay there anymore. It sort of spreads. One day it’s my cousin, like if she sends a short text or seems a little distant, I’ll start wondering if she’s upset with me or if I did something wrong. Then the next minute it’s work, like worrying I’ll make a mistake on a support call or not explain something clearly and then it’ll reflect badly on me. And then it jumps back to money, like how I’m ever going to save enough or move forward with my life.

So I don’t know if there’s one single area where it originates now. It feels more like my mind just keeps moving from one possible problem to the next, and each one feels urgent while I’m thinking about it.

Same with mentoring sessions—I’ve missed several because the idea of showing up and being “on” felt like too much, even though I know those are meaningful and I don’t want to be unreliable there either.

So yes, it’s definitely interfering. Not every single day in some dramatic way, but enough that I’m noticing consequences, and other people probably are too.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent and excessive worry about everyday things for at least 6 months
doctor.question: Have you been experiencing these worries about everyday things for more than 6 months?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about nine months, since the condo loan started moving toward foreclosure.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the worries have been occurring, specifically whether they have lasted more than 6 months.

patient.answer:
Yes. It’s been more than six months. I’d say about nine months now, if I’m counting from when the condo loan started moving toward foreclosure.

That was sort of the point where the worrying stopped feeling like a normal reaction to a stressful situation and started becoming… I don’t know, like a constant background noise. At first I told myself, “Of course I’m worried, anyone would be,” because the foreclosure stuff was genuinely scary and practical and real. But then months kept going by, and even when I wasn’t dealing with that exact issue in the moment, the worry was still there and started attaching itself to everything else.

So yes, roughly nine months. It feels like long enough that I can’t really tell myself it’s just a bad week anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of excessive anxiety about everyday things that is difficult to control
doctor.question: Do you find it difficult to stop worrying about everyday things once you've started?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: Even when I tell myself I've already checked the spreadsheet or sent the email, the thoughts keep looping, and one 'what if' turns into five more before I can pull myself back.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry is difficult to stop once it begins, which directly matches uncontrollable worry.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. That’s one of the most frustrating parts, honestly, because I can tell myself logically, “You already checked that,” or “You already sent the email,” or “There’s nothing else you can do about it right now,” but it doesn’t really stop.

Like with work stuff, I’ll check a spreadsheet and see that the information is there, and then a few minutes later I’ll have this thought like, “What if I missed a row?” or “What if I typed something wrong?” And then I go back and check it again, and sometimes even after that, my brain still doesn’t feel satisfied. It’s like the worry doesn’t accept evidence, if that makes sense.

And one “what if” turns into another really quickly. I’ll start with, “What if I made a mistake in that email?” and then it becomes, “What if the person misunderstands it?” and then, “What if my manager notices?” and then, “What if everyone thinks I’m careless?” It can spiral before I even realize how far it’s gone.

I do try to pull myself back, but it takes effort, and sometimes I feel like I’m arguing with my own mind. Like I know I’m overthinking, but knowing that doesn’t automatically make it stop.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worries are predominantly focused on a specific area or are more generalized
doctor.question: Are your worries usually about one specific type of thing, like work or finances, or do they seem to jump around between lots of different things?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My worry doesn't stay on the condo anymore; it jumps from whether my cousin is upset with me, to whether I'll make a mistake on a support call, to how I'll ever save money or move forward with my life.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worries are limited to one area or spread across many different everyday concerns, which directly matches excessive anxiety and worry about a number of events or activities.

patient.answer:
It definitely jumps around. It started with the condo, because that was the big obvious thing, and for a while I could kind of point to that and say, “Okay, this is what I’m worried about.” But now it doesn’t stay there at all.

It’ll move from something financial, like how I’m ever supposed to save money or get back on track or move forward with my life, to something totally different, like whether my cousin is upset with me because she texted a little shorter than usual. And then I’ll start replaying what I said to her, wondering if I sounded dismissive or if I forgot something important.

And then at work it’ll become, “What if I make a mistake on this support call?” or “What if I don’t explain the fix clearly enough?” or “What if they think I’m incompetent?” It’s like my brain is always looking for the next place to land. So no, it’s not just one category anymore. It’s finances, relationships, work, the future—just kind of everything rotating through.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's worries are predominantly about one specific type of thing
doctor.question: Are your worries usually about one specific area of your life, such as work or relationships?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My worry doesn't stay on the condo anymore; it jumps from whether my cousin is upset with me, to whether I'll make a mistake on a support call, to how I'll ever save money or move forward with my life.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry is limited to one area or occurs across multiple areas of life, which directly matches excessive worry about a number of events or activities.

patient.answer:
No, it’s not usually just one area anymore. I mean, it started with the condo, so for a while I could tell myself, “This is financial stress, that makes sense.” But now it doesn’t stay there. It jumps around a lot.

Like I’ll be thinking about the condo or money, and then suddenly it turns into, “How am I ever going to save anything?” or “How am I supposed to move forward with my life if I’m always trying to catch up?” And then later the same day I’ll be stuck wondering if my cousin is upset with me because her text sounded a little short, and I’ll replay what I said to see if I did something wrong.

And at work it’ll be something else completely, like worrying I’m going to make a mistake on a support call or explain something badly and the person will think I don’t know what I’m doing. So… yeah, it moves between finances, family or relationships, work, the future. It doesn’t really stay in one lane.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of muscle tension as a physical symptom
doctor.question: Do you often notice muscle tension, such as clenching your jaw or tightening your fists, when you're feeling anxious or worried?

target_item.name: Restlessness_Tension
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I feel wound up almost all the time, like my body is bracing for the next bad thing even when I'm just sitting at my desk or trying to enjoy dance night.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical tension when anxious, which fits the restlessness/tension symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I do notice that, though I don’t always catch it right away. It’s more like I’ll suddenly realize my whole body has been tense for who knows how long. Like I’m sitting at my desk, not doing anything physically stressful, just answering tickets or reading something, and my shoulders are up or my body feels kind of locked in place.

It feels like I’m wound up almost all the time, honestly. Like my body is bracing for the next bad thing even when nothing is actually happening in that moment. I could be trying to focus on work, or even doing something that’s supposed to be fun, like dance night, and there’s still this tight, on-edge feeling underneath it.

It’s not always dramatic, but it’s constant enough that I notice it. Like I’m not fully relaxed very often. My body acts like it’s waiting for something to go wrong.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's anxiety is generalized or focused on a specific area
doctor.question: Is there one particular thing that you worry about more than anything else?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My worry doesn't stay on the condo anymore; it jumps from whether my cousin is upset with me, to whether I'll make a mistake on a support call, to how I'll ever save money or move forward with my life.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the worry is focused on one main concern or spread across different events and areas of life, which matches excessive anxiety and worry about multiple activities.

patient.answer:
I guess if I had to pick, the condo is still the one that feels like the original “big” worry, because that’s where all of this seemed to start. But it doesn’t really stay there anymore, so it’s hard to say there’s just one thing.

It’s more like the condo or money will be the doorway into everything else. I’ll start thinking about finances, like how I’m supposed to save money again or move forward with my life, and then somehow my brain jumps to something completely different. Like I’ll suddenly be worrying that my cousin is upset with me because her text sounded off, and then I’m replaying what I said and wondering if I did something wrong.

And then at work it shifts again, like, “What if I make a mistake on this support call?” or “What if I explain something badly and they think I’m incompetent?” So… the condo might be the biggest concrete thing, but honestly the worry doesn’t stay attached to one particular thing anymore. It kind of spreads out to whatever my brain can grab onto next.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of obsessive thoughts or compulsions to differentiate between generalized anxiety disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder
doctor.question: Do you have any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to ignore them or make them stop?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: Even when I tell myself I've already checked the spreadsheet or sent the email, the thoughts keep looping, and one 'what if' turns into five more before I can pull myself back.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about repetitive thoughts that persist despite attempts to ignore or stop them, which directly matches difficulty controlling worry.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. It’s like the thought doesn’t just come up once and then pass. It keeps circling back even after I’ve tried to reassure myself.

Like with work, I’ll tell myself, “You already sent the email, it was fine,” or “You already checked that spreadsheet,” but then a few minutes later I’m thinking, “What if I missed something?” And then that turns into, “What if someone notices before I do?” and then, “What if they think I’m careless?” and then it kind of branches out from there.

It’s frustrating because I can usually see, logically, that I’m repeating myself. I’ll know I’ve already checked something or already thought through it, but it doesn’t feel settled. My mind keeps looping back to it anyway, and one little “what if” turns into five more before I can really pull myself out of it. Sometimes I can stop it for a bit, but it’s like my brain just picks it back up again.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worries are predominantly related to one area or are more generalized
doctor.question: Are your worries usually focused on one main area of concern or do they cover a wide range of topics?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My worry doesn't stay on the condo anymore; it jumps from whether my cousin is upset with me, to whether I'll make a mistake on a support call, to how I'll ever save money or move forward with my life.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worries are limited to one area or spread across many topics, which directly matches excessive anxiety and worry about a number of events or activities.

patient.answer:
It covers a pretty wide range now. I mean, the condo was the main thing at first, and it still kind of sits in the background as this big unresolved thing, but the worry doesn’t stay neatly in that one box anymore.

It’ll start with something practical, like money or whether I’m ever going to be able to save properly again or move forward with my life, and then suddenly it’s about something totally different. Like I’ll be thinking about finances, and then my mind jumps to my cousin, like, “Was she annoyed with me?” or “Did I say something weird?” just because a text sounded a little short.

And then at work it’ll switch again. I’ll be on a support call or about to respond to someone and start thinking, “What if I make a mistake?” or “What if I explain it badly and they think I don’t know what I’m doing?” So it’s not really one main area anymore. It kind of bounces around to whatever feels like it could go wrong next.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worries are realistically based on their current situation
doctor.question: Do you think your worries are usually about things that could realistically happen, or are they often about unlikely scenarios?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My worry doesn't stay on the condo anymore; it jumps from whether my cousin is upset with me, to whether I'll make a mistake on a support call, to how I'll ever save money or move forward with my life.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the nature and realism of the patient's worries, which most directly relates to excessive anxiety and worry across events or activities.

patient.answer:
I think that’s what makes it confusing, because a lot of them are technically realistic. Like, it’s not impossible that my cousin could be upset with me, or that I could make a mistake on a support call, or that money could be tight and I’ll struggle to save again. Those things could happen.

But the way my mind treats them feels bigger than the actual situation, if that makes sense. A short text from my cousin turns into me wondering if I damaged the relationship somehow. One work call turns into, “What if I mess this up and everyone thinks I’m bad at my job?” And then the condo or money stuff becomes this whole spiral about how I’m ever going to move forward with my life.

So I wouldn’t say they’re always totally unrealistic scenarios. It’s more that my worry grabs onto things that are possible, and then it stretches them out until they feel much more threatening than they probably are.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worries are excessive and uncontrollable
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're able to control your worries most of the time?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: Even when I tell myself I've already checked the spreadsheet or sent the email, the thoughts keep looping, and one 'what if' turns into five more before I can pull myself back.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks whether the worries can be controlled most of the time, which matches difficulty stopping or controlling worry.

patient.answer:
Not most of the time, no. I can sometimes interrupt them for a little bit, but it doesn’t feel like I’m really in control of them.

Like, I’ll tell myself, “Okay, I already checked the spreadsheet,” or “I already sent that email, and it looked fine,” and I’ll try to move on. And for maybe a few minutes I can focus on something else. But then the thought comes back, almost like it was waiting there. It’s not even always a new concern — it’s the same thing looping again, like, “But what if you missed something?” or “What if you sent it with the wrong attachment?” or “What if someone notices and thinks you’re careless?”

And then once that starts, it doesn’t stay as one thought. One “what if” turns into five more before I can really pull myself back. I’ll know I’m doing it, too, which is the frustrating part. I’ll be sitting there thinking, “You already went over this,” but it still doesn’t feel settled. It’s like reassurance only works briefly, and then my mind starts arguing with it again. So I wouldn’t say I can control it most of the time. I can try to manage it, but it often feels like it keeps going on its own.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worries are typically about the future
doctor.question: Do you usually worry about things that might happen in the future?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My worry doesn't stay on the condo anymore; it jumps from whether my cousin is upset with me, to whether I'll make a mistake on a support call, to how I'll ever save money or move forward with my life.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the worries are about possible future events, which directly relates to expectant apprehension and excessive worry about multiple things that might happen.

patient.answer:
Yes, mostly. It’s very often about what might happen next, or what something could turn into. Like, it doesn’t just stay on the condo anymore, even though that’s still there in the background. My mind will jump ahead to, “What if I can’t save money again?” or “What if I never really get back on track or move forward with my life?”

And then it’ll jump to people, like with my cousin — if she seems a little off or sends a short reply, I start worrying that maybe she’s upset with me, and then I’m imagining what that means later, like maybe things will become awkward or I’ll have damaged the relationship somehow.

Or at work, before or during a support call, I’ll start thinking ahead like, “What if I make a mistake?” or “What if I don’t explain something clearly?” It’s not always something that has happened. It’s more like my brain keeps scanning for the next thing that could go wrong, and then I’m already reacting to it as if it’s about to happen.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worries are primarily focused on a specific area of their life
doctor.question: Is there a particular area of your life where your worries seem to originate or concentrate most frequently?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My worry doesn't stay on the condo anymore; it jumps from whether my cousin is upset with me, to whether I'll make a mistake on a support call, to how I'll ever save money or move forward with my life.
target_item.reason: The question asks where the worries concentrate or originate, which relates most directly to the pattern of excessive worry across multiple life areas such as the condo, relationships, work, money, and the future.

patient.answer:
It used to feel like the condo was the main thing, or at least that was the easiest thing to point to. Like, if someone asked me what I was stressed about, I could say, “Oh, it’s the condo situation,” and that would sound concrete.

But honestly, it doesn’t really stay there anymore. It sort of spreads. One day it’s my cousin, like if she sends a short text or seems a little distant, I’ll start wondering if she’s upset with me or if I did something wrong. Then the next minute it’s work, like worrying I’ll make a mistake on a support call or not explain something clearly and then it’ll reflect badly on me. And then it jumps back to money, like how I’m ever going to save enough or move forward with my life.

So I don’t know if there’s one single area where it originates now. It feels more like my mind just keeps moving from one possible problem to the next, and each one feels urgent while I’m thinking about it.

The patient's worries are not limited to one specific area and are accompanied by physical symptoms like muscle tension, which further supports this diagnosis.
